title: Your Analysis Routine
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/0/bo: **Top-Down analysis** means you always start from the **largest timeframe** and work your way down step by step: trend first, then the level, then the entry. Starting on the 5-minute usually gets you tangled in **noise**.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/1/bo: **Step 1 — daily:** the main trend and the big levels. **Step 2 — 4-hour:** the setup and entry zone. **Step 3 — 1-hour or 15-minute:** the trigger, entry point and stop loss.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/1/ex: Buy with a stop below the setup
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/2/pr: Put the steps of top-down analysis in order.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/2/it: Main trend on the weekly or daily
Setup and entry zone on the 4-hour
Trigger and stop loss on the 1-hour
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/2/ex: Each step is finer than the last: first the big picture (trend and levels), then the setup, and finally the precise entry timing.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/3/pr: Step one: this is EUR/USD's daily chart. What do you see?
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/3/op: An uptrend and a pullback to support
A downtrend and a support break
A range with no clear level
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/3/ex: The highs and lows keep rising, and price is back at 1.0850: the old high that's now acting as support. Time to drop to a lower timeframe.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/4/pr: Final step: on the 1-hour, price printed a bullish engulfing inside the daily support zone. What's your decision?
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/4/ex: The daily trend is up, price is on daily support, and the 1-hour gave a buy trigger: all three steps agree. A continuation up is more likely, with a stop below the support zone.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/5/ti: Write your analysis in one sentence
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/5/bo: The output of a top-down analysis should be **one clear sentence**: "Daily up, pullback to 1.0850 support, waiting for a buy trigger on the 1-hour." If you can't write that sentence, your analysis isn't finished yet.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/6/st: In top-down analysis, you first find the trigger on the 5-minute, then check the daily to confirm it.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/6/ex: It's the other way around: daily first (trend and levels), then the lower timeframes. Starting on the 5-minute makes you hunt for reasons to back a decision you've already made.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/7/se: In top-down analysis, you take your trade direction from the ___ timeframe and your entry point from the ___ timeframe.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l1/steps/7/ex: The higher timeframe gives the direction and the big picture; the lower timeframe gives the exact entry moment and where the stop goes.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/0/bo: Pilots run through a **checklist** before every flight, even after thousands of hours in the air. A checklist stops **emotional entries**: if one item isn't ticked, there's no trade.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/1/bo: A simple multi-timeframe checklist. The answer to **every item** must be "yes" before you enter.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/1/ex: 2. Is price at a higher-TF level?
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/2/pr: The daily trend is up and price is on 4-hour support, but no trigger has appeared on the 1-hour yet. What does the checklist say?
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/2/op: I buy right now with full size
I sell because there's no trigger
I enter without a stop loss
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/2/ex: Item three isn't ticked. The level might break; a trigger shows the reaction has actually started.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/3/pr: Put the checklist items in the right order.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/3/it: Log the trade in your journal
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/3/ex: From big picture to details: trend, level, trigger and risk management. Then, after you enter, log the trade so you can review it later.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/4/pr: Your account is $2,000 and you want to risk 1%. Your EUR/USD stop is 20 pips, and each pip is worth $10 for 1 standard lot. What's the right size?
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/4/ex: 1% of 2,000 = $20. With 0.1 lot each pip is $1, and 20 pips × $1 = $20: exactly your allowed risk.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/5/bo: Stop loss beyond the **lower-timeframe setup**, target at the **next higher-timeframe level**. If the risk-to-reward is below your rule (say, 1:2), even the best setup gets **rejected**. A trade you don't take can't lose you money.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/6/pr: Your rule is at least 1:2. With this entry, stop loss and take profit, is the trade a go?
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/6/op: Yes; risk is 20 pips and reward is 60 (1:3)
No; the risk is bigger than the reward
Yes; because no stop loss is needed
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/6/ex: Entry 1.2720, stop 1.2700 (20 pips) and take profit 1.2780 (60 pips): 60 ÷ 20 = 3. A 1:3 ratio beats your minimum.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/7/pr: The daily is up and price has reached 4-hour support; only the trigger is missing. Tap the 15-minute candle that fired the buy trigger.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/7/ex: This hammer's long lower wick on 4-hour support shows buyers have stepped in. Now every item on the checklist is ticked.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/8/st: If just one checklist item isn't ticked but your gut feels great, entering makes sense.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l2/steps/8/ex: The checklist exists for exactly these moments, when feelings try to replace rules. One missing item means wait.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/0/bo: Pro traders don't **predict**; they write **scenarios**: "If price does this, I'll do that." One **main scenario** (with the higher timeframe) and one **alternative scenario** for when the level breaks.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/1/bo: EUR/USD's daily trend is up and price is nearing the 1.0850 support. Both outcomes are written down in advance, so when the market moves you just **execute** instead of rethinking everything.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/1/ex: If the daily closes below it
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/2/pr: Your main scenario: "If the 1.0850 support holds and a buy trigger appears on the 1-hour, I buy." Now look at what happened. What do you do?
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/2/ex: Price reached 1.0850, bounced with a hammer, and the next candle confirmed it: the main scenario's conditions are met. You enter as planned, with a stop below the hammer's low.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/3/pr: This time, price closed below the 1.0850 support on the daily. What do your scenarios say?
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/3/op: Buy canceled; I step aside and reanalyze
I buy anyway, since the main scenario was a buy
I move my stop lower so it doesn't get hit
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/3/ex: A daily close below support is exactly the alternative scenario's condition. You already decided the buy is canceled here; just follow through.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/4/bo: Every scenario has an **Invalidation** point: a price that, if crossed, means your idea was wrong. Your stop loss usually goes right there. Write your scenario **before the trade, with a calm mind**, not in the heat of the market.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/5/se: Every scenario needs an ___ point: a price where, if it's crossed, you ___ the idea.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/5/ex: The invalidation point is the price that shows your analysis was wrong. That's where you let go of the idea instead of clinging to it.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/6/st: An alternative scenario helps you follow your plan when a level breaks, instead of making an emotional decision.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/6/ex: The market always has another possibility. When you've already written "here's what I do if the level breaks", at the moment of the break you just execute, and fear or hope don't get to decide.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/7/pr: Put the steps of writing and executing a scenario in order.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/7/it: Analyze trend and levels on the higher timeframe
Write the main scenario with an invalidation point
Execute only after a lower-timeframe trigger
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/7/ex: Big picture first, then two scenarios with clear conditions, and finally execution only once the conditions are met.
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/8/pr: BTC: daily up, 4-hour support at 62,000 and the previous daily high at 68,000. On the 1-hour, a buy trigger fired at 62,500 and the setup low is 61,500. Which plan is complete and sensible?
lessons/multi-timeframe-u3-l3/steps/8/ex: Direction from the daily, zone from the 4-hour, and entry from the 1-hour trigger. Risk is about $1,000 and reward $5,500, roughly 1:5. The other options either have no stop or get the logic backwards.
